_comment: Every entry is a control this project claims to have, and the exact edit that
should break it. `node scripts/mutate.mjs --all` applies each one to the real
source, runs the real suite, and demands that the named test goes red.
AUDIT-PROTOCOL.md §6: a green suite is evidence that nothing currently
disagrees with a control, not that the control exists. This file is where that
distinction is made mechanical -- and where 'nobody audits the auditor' (§7) is
answered, because each mutation is stated precisely enough to be re-run by
ADD AN ENTRY WHEN YOU ADD A CONTROL. Not later, and not only when a control
looks fragile: the two worst defects of 2026-09-03 were both in code written
that same hour specifically to enforce verification honesty, and both looked
finished. `find` must match EXACTLY ONCE or the run reports INCONCLUSIVE.
The `expect` field is a substring of the test name that must appear among the
failures. Without it, ANY red suite would count as the control working -- which
is how a mutation that broke something unrelated gets recorded as proof.

mutations.guards: the modelled ground extends far enough that its own outer edge is beyond the range where the sea bed still reads through the water -- the original tray was visible because the ground stopped at 19.5 km, not because it had an edge at all
mutations.note: This entry SURVIVED once, and correctly. Its expect still named 'the ground reaches further than the water', a test renamed when the seabed-ring invariant was fixed. The mutation turned the suite red, but not on the named test, and the runner refused to score that as a pass. An expect is a reference to a test name, and renaming a test silently breaks it -- which is now checked at startup.
mutations.expect: the ground's own edge is far enough out

mutations.guards: the apron's coarse grid lands exactly on the fine mesh's edges, so the two abut instead of gapping or overlapping
mutations.note: This mutation could not bite at all until APRON_STEP_MULTIPLE moved into WORLD. The test used to compute the step itself, so no change to the renderer could fail it. Writing this entry is what found that.
mutations.expect: the apron grid lands exactly on the modelled rectangle's edges

mutations.guards: each cloud deck owns its material, so the low one can fade while the high one is still overhead
mutations.expect: the decks fade INDEPENDENTLY

mutations.guards: a deck you have climbed above stops drawing, instead of rendering its far rim as a white crescent
mutations.expect: at the orbit Mark was flying

mutations.guards: sand is bounded by distance from the coastline, not by height alone, so a slowly-rising shelf does not get painted as a 975 m sandbar
mutations.expect: the thresholds are BUILT metres

mutations.guards: both pages bloom the same world the same way, because the renderer uses the shared BLOOM object rather than a copy of its values
mutations.note: Mutating to an equal-valued literal, not a different one: the point is that a COPY is the defect, even when the numbers happen to match today. That is precisely how the two pages drifted apart in the first place.
mutations.expect: the tuned render values are what they are meant to be

mutations.guards: props.js resolves every manifest id by its own name, so prop-models.js does not need a second table that must agree with it
mutations.expect: the LIBRARY declares the join

mutations.guards: every building on a block shares one architectural era, so variety is BETWEEN streets rather than within them -- this is the single decision that stops a rules-driven city reading as clones on a grid
mutations.note: The wrong version is one character shorter and passes any test that only checks 'a character was assigned'. Rolling per building makes every street an even mix of all four eras, so at the altitude you actually view the city from, every street looks like every other street: randomising per building produces UNIFORMITY. This mutation is the difference, and it is measured on the real 26 km world rather than on a fixture.
mutations.expect: not one block carries two architectural characters

mutations.guards: the first and last plot in a row are end units with one party wall, and everything between them is a middle unit with two -- without this a terrace is ten identical houses standing near each other
mutations.expect: the ends of a row are ends

mutations.guards: a terrace is sized DOWN to whole 8 m units that fit the plot, so it never hangs over the boundary and gets refused after the work of building it
mutations.expect: terrace units fill the plot without overhanging it

mutations.guards: a shop or high-street terrace is only placed where it actually has street frontage, so a corner shop is on a corner rather than buried mid-row with its shopfront facing a party wall
mutations.expect: a shop only appears where it has street frontage

mutations.guards: footprint.js's "terrace" VERDICT (ground that steps) is translated to the asset lane's "stepped" foundation, so it is never confused with the "bld-terrace" TYPOLOGY (a row of houses), which is an unrelated thing wearing the same word
mutations.expect: every foundation the table emits is one the asset lane builds

mutations.guards: a footprint's sample grid is capped at 56 m however wide the footprint is, so a 3.5 km runway cannot step over a river lying across it -- 56 m is the full width of the narrowest water in waterways.js, read from it rather than picked
mutations.note: The comment on sampleGrid claimed 'never coarser than TARGET_SPACING'. Measured, it was 8 m at 200 m wide, 24 m at 600 m and 140 m at 3,500 m -- true below about 100 m and false everywhere it mattered. The ceiling costs nothing at any size except the single largest footprint in the world, where it is 6.1x.
mutations.expect: sees a 60 m trench that used to fall between its samples

mutations.guards: a plot of a class that declares a module is a whole number of those 8 m cells wide, so a terrace actually tiles instead of standing as detached houses showing each other their blank party walls
mutations.note: Measured before PLOT_CLASSES declared a module: 0 of 5,257 TERRACE plots could tile. Mean plot width 12 m against an 8 m unit left a 4.00 m gap between every adjacent pair. Every end-left/middle/end-right variant the asset lane built was defeated by the subdivision, and the result would have read as a rendering bug rather than a planning one.
mutations.expect: every row-class plot is a whole number of 8 m cells

mutations.guards: a variant group is seeded by its own key, so every member gets byte-identical geometry and the city can be drawn as a few hundred InstancedMeshes instead of one mesh per building
mutations.note: Seeding each building from its plot id sounds like more variety and is what makes instancing impossible: 20,472 buildings would be 20,472 draw calls against the 14 instanced buckets the renderer uses today. Measured, grouping by SITUATION collapses the city to 244 variants at 1.48 M triangles.
mutations.expect: collapses to a few hundred instanceable variants

mutations.guards: the layout asks buildings.js whether a typology fits the plot BEFORE choosing it, instead of picking by weight and discovering the overhang at placement time
mutations.note: This entry exists because the first version of it SURVIVED. The predicate is optional (planCity defaults it to null), so every test in layout.test.ts ran the unfiltered path and disabling the filter changed nothing any test could see. A control only exercised by a script is not a control. The test now lives in layoutGeometry.test.ts, where buildings.js is available, and measures the difference: 3,552 overhangs without, 269 with.
mutations.expect: stops it overhanging

mutations.guards: layout-fits.js measures a candidate with the SAME seed the renderer will build it with, via the shared seedFor, so the building that was checked for fit is the building that gets built
mutations.note: Found by measurement, not by reasoning. The sizer briefly computed its own seed while planPlot used the variant key; since the seed drives the fallback size, the two disagreed and overhangs went 269 -> 556 with the whole suite green. The first version of THIS mutation also survived, because countOverhangs measured with the literal seed "measure" -- the same defect, committed by the test that was meant to catch it. Both are fixed; the mutation now reports 653 overhangs against a 409 ceiling. Find/replace and expect updated when askedFor was pulled out as its own function (H1's survivor fix): the overhang-count test alone could no longer catch this, because terrain tuning moved the measured figure (269 -> ~293) closer to the 409 ceiling, and 653 overhangs still sits under it. The new test asserts the CAUSE -- seed equality, exact over every placement -- rather than the consequence. (Merge note, Phase L: assets-lane independently edited this same entry against the pre-H1-refactor shape of layout-fits.js -- that target line no longer exists after the refactor, so main's version is kept; assets-lane's edit is superseded, not lost -- both were fixing the identical defect.)
mutations.expect: the seed layout-fits.js measured a placement with is the seed the renderer builds it with

mutations.guards: a row of module-class plots STARTS on an 8 m cell, so every building in the world has a whole-cell address rather than merely tiling against its own neighbours
mutations.note: Snapping the plot WIDTH was not enough. Measured, only 3 of 2,291 blocks begin on an 8 m boundary (median offset 2.80 m), so a perfectly tiling row still sat at a fractional cell address. Nothing looked wrong because the streets hide it -- but WORLD-RULES 3.2 declares the 8 m CELL as the module the world is built on and grid.js hands out addresses on it. After the fix: 14,378 of 14,378 module-class plots start on a cell.
mutations.expect: STARTS on an 8 m cell

mutations.guards: the back row of a block is turned 180 degrees, so it addresses the street it fronts instead of showing it a back garden
mutations.note: subdivideBlock lays two rows back to back fronting opposite streets, and models are built facing +z. Unrotated, 9,845 of 19,725 buildings -- half the city -- would present their front door, porch and shopfront to the rear boundary. Nothing would look broken from the air, which is what makes it worth a control.
mutations.expect: back row faces the other way

mutations.guards: every row of the navigation pad draws itself with --nav-radius and --nav-shadow, so the pad reads as one instrument instead of a stack of chips with different corners
mutations.note: Mark: 'the nav is a mess from a looks standpoint ... it just looks disconnected from each other and random.' Measured, that was three different corner radii (11px on the strips, 10px on the readout, 50% on the dial) and two shadows across five rows. No single row was wrong, which is how they got there one at a time -- so the control is against the FOURTH one arriving.
mutations.expect: uses those tokens instead of its own numbers

mutations.guards: the pad's rows are border-box and full width, so their left AND right edges line up instead of each row sizing to its own content
mutations.note: Without border-box the 1px borders and the padding push each row past --nav-w by a different amount, and the ragged right edge returns by arithmetic rather than by anyone typing a width -- which is the version of this defect that would be hardest to see in a diff.
mutations.expect: edges line up

mutations.guards: canPlace takes the footprint's heights through a getter, so a candidate refused by the terrain or by what is already built never pays for a measurement it does not use -- and nothing can read the heights before they are taken
mutations.note: The measurement used to be eager, to close a real ordering hazard where a later step read `hi` as -Infinity and a 30 m tower was accepted onto a house lot. Eager fixed that and made every rejection pay 676 probes. MEASURED on findGround for an unplaceable spec: 12,142,980 heightAt calls in 11.0 s, over 17,910 candidates. After: 35,820 calls in 0.46 s -- 339x fewer probes, same answer. The getter closes both problems, where simply moving the loop later would have reopened the first.
mutations.find: // 1. DOES THE LAND ITSELF FORBID IT?
mutations.replace:
groundRange();
    // 1. DOES THE LAND ITSELF FORBID IT?
mutations.expect: does not pay to measure the ground first

mutations.guards: waterAt reports the depth AT THE POINT, derived from the channel's own surface level, so a hull at the bank does not read the mid-channel figure
mutations.note: MEASURED on river-mid before: bed 59.31 m at the centreline climbing to 66.34 m at 50 m out, and 5.85 m of declared depth reported at every one of them. The function even computed heightAt and discarded it, under a comment describing a surface at bed + depth that nothing calculated.
mutations.expect: a level surface, a sloping bed, and dry banks

mutations.guards: ground inside a channel's envelope but above its water line is dry land, so a river has banks rather than vertical walls and nothing floats up a shelving bed
mutations.note: The first version of this control SURVIVED, and finding out why exposed a third defect: waterwayInfoAt reported the manifest's untapered halfWidth while membership was decided by the tapered one, so the test's walk was escaping the rectangle rather than reaching a waterline. It reports the deciding figure now.
mutations.expect: a level surface, a sloping bed, and dry banks

mutations.guards: the working tree holds the same bytes as the repository, so `git add` has nothing to convert and never rewrites a file another process is reading
mutations.note: `* text=auto` stores LF and checks out CRLF on Windows. MEASURED: one commit of small edits reported 66,043 insertions across 12 files, and `git add -A` renormalising the 4 MB public/tier-models.js during a mutate run made esbuild read it mid-rewrite -- a syntax error at 4722:40 that does not exist, 3 test files failing to build, and 14 consecutive INCONCLUSIVE results reported as '10 of 24 controls proved they exist'.
mutations.expect: the working tree and the repository hold the same bytes

mutations.guards: the model catalogue is linked from the front door, so a player can reach the 2,400 models by clicking rather than by typing a filename
mutations.note: The worst defect found in this repository, and it was not a bug -- everything worked. Six pages existed in public/ and exactly ONE was reachable. An unreachable page is not an error, it is an absence, and absences do not throw, which is why no test would ever have caught it. This one walks the links.
mutations.expect: reachable from the front door

mutations.guards: every page a player can land on links back to the front door, so none of them is a trap
mutations.note: The first version of this control accepted EITHER a back-to-caliper class OR a link home, and a mutation renaming the class correctly survived -- the href was still there. That exposed the weakness in the other direction: a page carrying the class with a broken href would have passed on the strength of a CSS class name. A class is decoration; an href is the way out.
mutations.expect: way back

mutations.guards: a layer is refused unless it is storable data, so a world can be saved, sent, cloned and attributed
mutations.note: The first version relied on JSON.stringify failing on a function. It does not -- it silently DROPS it, so a layer carrying a closure round-tripped with the same edit count and was accepted, then lost the player's work on save with no message. Found by this exact mutation surviving.
mutations.expect: plain data that survives being stored

mutations.guards: cloning a world deep-copies its layers, so editing your copy cannot reach back into the world you copied from
mutations.note: The first version spread each edit but shared its payload object. Editing a clone would have silently edited the original -- the worst possible version of this feature and invisible until someone noticed their world had changed. The test only compared layer COUNTS, so the mutation survived until it was strengthened to mutate a payload.
mutations.expect: same base and a copy of the work

mutations.guards: a later layer overrides an earlier one PER OP, so a move and a retint by two different authors coexist on the same object
mutations.note: Whole-object replacement would make collaboration impossible and undo destructive: the newest edit would erase every other change anyone had made to that thing.
mutations.find: for (const e of this.editsFor(address)) byOp.set(e.op, e);
mutations.replace: for (const e of this.editsFor(address)) { byOp.clear(); byOp.set(e.op, e); }
mutations.expect: independent changes coexist

mutations.guards: a stored layer that fails to load is reported rather than dropped, so a player's work never vanishes from their world in silence
mutations.find: if (bad) errors.push({ id: layer && layer.id, reason: bad });
mutations.expect: REPORTED, not silently dropped

mutations.guards: a remove beats every other edit to the same address, whatever order they arrived in
mutations.expect: removal wins outright

mutations.guards: seed 0 reproduces the pre-seed noise field byte for byte, so adding seeding did not silently move the world every measured number in this repo describes
mutations.note: The seed is mixed in by MULTIPLICATION precisely so it contributes exactly zero at seed 0. Most of this suite asserts properties rather than values, so a terrain that shifted by a metre would go on passing while invalidating 20,624 plots, 480 variants, 1.45 M triangles, the zoning percentiles and the airport's 11,041 dry sample points. The identity is pinned against the original expression written out longhand. Find/replace updated when hash2 started converting its own seed with seedToInt (A2b) -- the line moved from "Math.imul(seed, ...)" to "Math.imul(s, ...)".
mutations.expect: reproduces the original noise field exactly

mutations.guards: createNoise binds its seed into every function it returns, so a named world is genuinely a different landmass rather than the same one under a new name
mutations.note: The first version of this mutation neutered only hash2 and valueNoise and left fbm seeded, so the world still differed and it SURVIVED -- a bad mutation, not a weak test. Targeting the single place the seed is resolved is what makes it bite. Find/replace widened to include the function signature when A2b made hash2 also call seedToInt(seed) into a same-named local -- the old one-line find matched twice (hash2 and createNoise) and would have scored INCONCLUSIVE.
mutations.find:
export function createNoise(seed = DEFAULT_SEED) {
  const s = seedToInt(seed);
mutations.replace:
export function createNoise(seed = DEFAULT_SEED) {
  const s = 0;
mutations.expect: different seed is a different world

mutations.guards: a LandField keeps the seed it was built with, so a named world is a genuinely different landmass rather than the same one relabelled
mutations.note: The seed lives on the FIELD rather than being threaded through every height call: heightAt is asked tens of millions of times per world build, and a parameter that must be passed at every call site is one somebody eventually forgets, producing a world that is half one place and half another.
mutations.expect: named seed is a genuinely different landmass

mutations.guards: makeHeightAt reads the field's seed and passes it to every shaping function, so seeding reaches the actual ground rather than stopping at the field object
mutations.note: An earlier version of this mutation neutered only edgeFalloff and SURVIVED -- cliffiness, shoreRampAt and reliefAt were still seeded, so the world still differed. A partial mutation proves nothing. KNOWN GAP: this pins that the seed reaches the shaping functions collectively, not that each one's seed is individually load-bearing.
mutations.find: const seed = field && Number.isFinite(field.seed) ? field.seed : DEFAULT_SEED;
mutations.expect: named seed is a genuinely different landmass

mutations.guards: generateWorld threads its seed into the plan (cityDemand, generateCityPlan, generateSettlement), not just the ground, so a named world gets a genuinely different street grid and zoning mix, not just different hills
mutations.note: Reassigns the seed AT ITS FIRST USE inside generateWorld rather than at one of the three downstream call sites -- the seed fans out to cityDemand, generateCityPlan and generateSettlement independently, and settlement plots alone still differ by seed even if only the downtown path (generateCityPlan) is broken, so a mutation on that one call site alone would SURVIVE against a whole-world fingerprint. This targets the single point all three pass through.
mutations.find: const demandAt = heightAt ? cityDemand(heightAt, seed) : null;
mutations.replace: const demandAt = heightAt ? cityDemand(heightAt, seed = DEFAULT_SEED) : null;
mutations.expect: a named seed lays out a genuinely different street grid

mutations.guards: generateWorld's returned districts array deep-copies each district's nested bounds object, so mutating one world's district bounds cannot reach another world's copy or the frozen spec
mutations.note: A shallow { ...d } copies the top-level fields but leaves bounds pointing at DISTRICTS[i]s own object -- every world built in the process shared one bounds object per district until this was fixed.
mutations.expect: mutating one world's district bounds does not reach another world's, or the spec

mutations.guards: createWorlds toJSON includes the layer stack, not just the seed, so a stored world can rebuild with its edits intact
mutations.note: The whole point of A4 is that a world round-trips -- a toJSON that dropped layers would serialise a world that forgets every edit on the next load, silently.
mutations.expect: rebuilds to the same fingerprint

mutations.guards: load() reports a stored record that is not valid JSON, instead of swallowing the parse failure and quietly returning what looks like a valid, empty world
mutations.note: The mutation replaces the reported failure with a fabricated, VALID-shaped result (a real string seed, empty layers) rather than just deleting the return -- a mutation that left data malformed would still get caught by the very next validation check for an unrelated reason, which would prove nothing about this specific line.
mutations.find: return { ok: false, reason: `stored record for "${worldId}" is not valid JSON -- refusing to load it as an empty world` };
mutations.expect: is REPORTED, not silently dropped

mutations.guards: applyLayers calls world.resolve only for addresses the layer stack actually touched, never once per placement -- the cost of having layers scales with the size of the edit, not the size of the world
mutations.note: Re-resolving every placement would still produce a visually correct result (an untouched address resolves to an unedited state), so a happy-path visibility test would not catch this -- only counting resolve() calls does.
mutations.replace: for (const p of placements) { const address = p.plotId;
mutations.expect: resolve is called exactly once per touched address

mutations.guards: an overridden placement is pushed to overridden and EXCLUDED from instanced, so the shared InstancedMesh group never sees it -- otherwise it draws from the old shared geometry as well as its own override, twice
mutations.note: Dropping the else keeps the if-branch's push but ALSO falls through to the instanced push, exactly the failure mode named in the ledger: apply the override without removing it from the group.
mutations.expect: an overridden plot is absent from its original variant's instance group

mutations.guards: an override naming a model id that is not in the registry is refused BY THAT ID, never silently drawn as a fallback shape
mutations.note: The mutation is literally the temptation the ledger names: fall back to a default model on unknown id.
mutations.replace: const model = registry.get(modelId) || { ok: true, geometry: { attributes: {} }, measured: { triangles: 12 } };
mutations.expect: a layer referencing an unknown model id is refused at resolve

mutations.guards: a pick's plotId is the actual plot id, not the containing block's id -- the two ids look similar (both plan-derived strings) so a swap would not throw, only quietly point every edit at the wrong granularity of object
mutations.note: The ledger names this exact failure mode: return the nearest block instead of the plot.
mutations.replace:
current = { ...index.addressAt(x, z) }; current.plotId = current.blockId;
      return current;
mutations.expect: a pick returns a real plot id that is present in the plan

mutations.guards: the requests text field is exactly what was typed -- never templated into a markup string, which is the one way the apps existing textContent-only display discipline could be defeated upstream
mutations.note: Wrapping the text in a span is the literal anti-pattern this module exists to never do.
mutations.expect: typed text that looks like HTML passes through byte-identical

mutations.guards: verifyGeneratedGeometry checks a response against the ACTUAL requested footprint, never a loosened or fabricated one -- a response that ignores the constraint fails verification rather than being repaired or waved through
mutations.note: This is the ledgers own failure mode for D4: a response that ignores the measured constraints must fail verification, not be silently accepted. Inflating the declared footprint before checking is exactly the kind of quiet repair that would let it through.
mutations.replace: return verifyModelSource(source, { w: prompt.constraints.footprint.w + 1000, d: prompt.constraints.footprint.d + 1000 }, evaluate, THREE);
mutations.expect: verification uses the REQUESTED footprint, never anything the response itself claims

mutations.guards: a failed verdict is described in words that say failed/refused, never smoothed into text that reads as a success -- the failure-floor item 1 this whole project is built to prevent, applied to one stage's own display text
mutations.note: The mutation reports success text regardless of the verdict, which is exactly shipping an unverified/failed change while reporting it as verified.
mutations.find: return { ok: false, text: `verification failed at ${v.stage}: ${v.reason}` };
mutations.expect: a failed verify is shown as a failed verify

mutations.guards: the persisted layer references its model by id only -- the generated source is never inlined into it, which is what keeps a layer storable, sendable and diffable as plain data
mutations.note: source is in scope in applyAndPersist (the caller has it right after D4s verify step) -- this mutation is the realistic accident of including it, not a strawman.
mutations.find: edits: [{ address: request.address, op: "replace", payload: { modelId } }],
mutations.replace: edits: [{ address: request.address, op: "replace", payload: { modelId, source } }],
mutations.expect: a verified model becomes a layer that references it BY ID, never inlining the source

mutations.guards: undoLayer re-saves the world after removing a layer, so the removal survives a reload instead of only existing in memory until the next persisted save brings the undone layer back
mutations.note: This is the actual gap end-to-end proof exists for: worldModel.test.ts already proves remove() itself works in isolation. What isolation cannot see is a removal that never gets persisted.
mutations.expect: the undo survives a reload

mutations.guards: changeSomethingQuest completes because the world's own layer stack actually holds an edit, never because a UI-set flag says so -- a quest that completes on a flag is a cutscene
mutations.note: Named in the plan as the single most important mutation in Phase E. Reading state.player.mode is exactly the shape of the failure this quest exists to refuse.
mutations.expect: setting a UI flag, with no real edit, does NOT complete the quest

mutations.guards: a locked/unloaded region refuses placement with a reason and a detail string, never a bare false -- an empty result and a locked region must never look alike
mutations.note: Ledger finding named directly in the plan: absence nobody can see. A bare false is indistinguishable from any other falsy 'nothing happened' signal; {ok:false, reason, detail} is not.
mutations.find: return { ok: false, reason: "locked", detail: `(${x.toFixed(0)}, ${z.toFixed(0)}) is in a part of the world that is not open yet` };
mutations.expect: loaded then unloaded, refuses again

mutations.guards: checkInputGuard reads its length cap from CONTROL_LIMITS.FREE_FORM_MAX_LENGTH, never a hard-coded number at the call site -- a hard-coded copy stops tracking the one limits object silently
mutations.note: This is the exact mutation G1 names in the plan: hard-code one -> the test names it.
mutations.expect: checkInputGuard reads FREE_FORM_MAX_LENGTH live from CONTROL_LIMITS

mutations.guards: filterPending actually removes mutations whose id is already recorded, so --resume does not re-run (and re-report) work a prior, killed session already proved
mutations.note: Without this, --resume would print resuming: N of 52 already done and then run all 52 again anyway -- the exact defect the harness fix exists to prevent.
mutations.expect: a results file with three ids recorded causes those three to be skipped

mutations.guards: CLAUDE.md's How to verify section names the real, current node/worker test counts -- pinned mechanically, the same way test/publicClaims.test.ts already pins the page's identical claim, closing the gap a blind audit found the file stale by 297 tests
mutations.note: Found by docs/audits/UMAA-phases-B-H.md (Finding 1, HIGH): CLAUDE.md claimed 571 node tests where 868 actually ran -- the document instructing a reader how to verify the project was itself unverified against the thing it names.
mutations.find: npm test            # 905 node tests + 12 worker tests
mutations.replace: npm test            # 906 node tests + 12 worker tests
mutations.expect: CLAUDE.md's verification line names the real test counts

mutations.guards: closeRegion on a whole-world-open grid (open === null) genuinely refuses with a reason, rather than silently reporting success for a region that was never load-tracked in the first place
mutations.note: Found untested by docs/audits/UMAA-phases-B-H.md (Finding 3): every prior closeRegion test used an explicit openRegions list; createWorld()'s own default (regions: null) -- the shape of every world built today -- reaches this branch and nothing exercised it.
mutations.find: return { ok: false, reason: `grid: cannot close "${name}" -- the whole world is open, not region-tracked` };
mutations.expect: closing a region on a whole-world-open grid (open === null) is refused

mutations.guards: a second createWorld() call for the same seed reuses the same LandField/heightAt object, not a fresh one -- the memoisation Finding 5 asked for, without which generateWorld's own heightAt-identity-keyed caches (cityDemand, placeFeatures) never hit on a repeat call
mutations.note: Found by docs/audits/UMAA-phases-B-H.md (Finding 5): createWorld() cost 2.3-2.7s per call and a repeat call with the identical seed was not materially cheaper, because a fresh LandField/heightAt was built every time.
mutations.expect: a second createWorld() call for the same seed reuses the same land

mutations.guards: the general aliasing test (test/worldAliasing.test.ts) subsumes the specific district-bounds test (test/worldSpec.test.ts) A3 wrote -- reintroducing A3's own shallow-copy bug (this time for the f/allow fields the original fix missed) must turn the GENERAL test red, not just be caught by luck
mutations.note: Named before the test was written, per instruction: reintroducing A3's shallow district copy (removing the f/allow deep-copy this session added alongside it) should turn test/worldAliasing.test.ts red, proving it subsumes the specific case rather than duplicating it.
mutations.expect: two worlds with the SAME seed share only the declared allow-list

mutations.guards: generateWorld copies each downtown plot's buildable rectangle, not just the plot itself -- generateCityPlan's own seed-keyed cache (A2b) means two same-seed worlds share the underlying city.plots array, so a shallow plot copy alone still aliases .buildable across both
mutations.note: Found by test/worldAliasing.test.ts: this was a live gap from A2b's own caching, never exercised until the general aliasing test walked two same-seed worlds and compared them.
mutations.expect: two worlds with the SAME seed share only the declared allow-list

mutations.guards: LandField freezes itself once built -- decision A, made explicit: sharing land across two same-seed worlds (Finding 5) is safe only because nothing can write through it
mutations.note: Verified empirically before this freeze was made permanent: the full 872-test suite was run once with it in place and passed unchanged, proving nothing in this codebase currently writes to a LandField after construction.
